appraisal_events.evidence: « Mais, Dieu merci, je ne la connais pas... C’est à Marie-Aynard qu’il faut demander cela. Elle la connaît et je me suis toujours demandé pourquoi. » — to which Mme de Marsantes answers « je confesse mes erreurs ».
appraisal_events.explanation: The duchesse deflects Villeparisis's question by publicly pointing at Mme de Marsantes as the one who compromises herself with Lady Israël, and Mme de Marsantes must accept the reproach and confess her error before the company.

appraisal_events.evidence: « En réalité Mme de Marsantes pensait que son fils n’aurait pas de permission... elle espérait, en ayant l’air de croire qu’elle l’eût trouvé ici, lui faire pardonner... toutes les visites qu’il ne lui avait pas faites », answered by « Robert ici ! Mais je n’ai pas même eu un mot de lui ».
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator lays bare Mme de Marsantes's calculated pretense on her son's behalf, and Villeparisis's flat, slightly aggrieved reply immediately defeats the maneuver while exposing Robert's neglect of his aunt.

status_effects.explanation: Named as the one who inexplicably keeps up the compromising acquaintance, she is put on the defensive and answers with a confession and a long self-justifying tirade.
The narrator's disclosure of her insincere stratagem, and its instant failure, lower her locally as a transparently maneuvering mother.
She controls the exchange with a dismissive witticism that costs her nothing and forces another woman to justify herself.
Absent and defended in advance, he is nonetheless shown up by his aunt's reply that she has not had a word from him since Balbec, after having been called a 'jeune fou' who talks nonsense.

ambiguities: The closing exchange can be read as diminishing Mme de Marsantes (her stratagem exposed and defeated) or Robert (his neglect of his aunt made public); the narrator's focus on her calculation favors her as the main target, with Robert affected through her.
